summary: Astro Farm is a free web farming game for children aged 8-12 in the Ecuadorian Andes. Players pick their real plot on a map, name their farm and guided by Pachita a Andean farmer character, read their land with NASA data: yearly rain, evaporation and root zone soil moisture. They choose crops suited to their altitude and planting season, water them when the soil is dry, haverst and then compare three crop rotation strategies, learning why alterating families and legumes keeps the soil healthy. Our slogan is: Today’s children will be tomorrow’s farmers.
details:
Astro Farm turns NASA climate data into a playful farming game. The flow is: pick your real plot on a satellite map → read your land (rain, evaporation, root-zone soil moisture, temperature) → choose a crop by altitude, family and planting month → plant on a 3D model of your terrain → advance time day by day with real weather → water when the soil is dry → harvest → compare three rotation strategies and earn a certificate. Pachita, an Andean farmer, explains every step in short dialogues with a child's voice, in Spanish or English.

How it works

  • NASA POWER Daily API (community AG, 2001–2024): rain, max/min temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation for the chosen point; the game replays real days.
  • NASA POWER Climatology: root-zone soil moisture (GWETROOT) month by month.
  • FAO-56 Penman-Monteith: reference evapotranspiration and a daily soil-water balance per crop stage (Kc), which decides when plants wilt and how much water they need.
  • Crop data for 13 Andean crops, planting seasons from INIAP and tested rotation cases from Ecuadorian field studies.
  • Rain was checked against 85 INAMHI weather stations above 2,000 m (monthly r = 0.51 for POWER/MERRA-2); calibration with IMERG and INAMHI is the next step.

Tools

Astro + TypeScript, three.js (3D terrain and crops), Leaflet (map), Python FastAPI on Vercel (science engine), SoilGrids (soil), Open-Meteo (terrain elevation), edge-tts (voice). Open source under the MIT License:

https://github.com/M47H3W1/pacha-bot

Benefits and impact

Children in rural Andean schools learn, by playing, how much water crops use and why rotating crops (especially with legumes) protects the soil. It runs on basic phones (3D and no-3D modes), costs almost nothing to operate and uses only open data.

What works today

A bilingual web game (ES/EN) with 3D and no-3D modes, 13 crops, three rotation strategies compared with explanations, and 20 automated tests. Next steps: pilot tests in rural schools and better local rain with IMERG + INAMHI calibration.

Creativity and considerations

We chose a game instead of a dashboard because the future farmers are today's kids. We designed for low literacy (voice and icons), low-end phones, Spanish and English, and honesty about data limits: NASA POWER cells are coarse, so we show ranges (dry, normal and rainy years) rather than exact predictions. AI-generated images are watermarked "IA"/"AI".
